ety.text: From Middle English after, from Old English æfter, from Proto-West Germanic *aftar, from Proto-Germanic *after, *aftiri, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epoteros (“further behind, further away”), from *h₂epo (“off, away”). Cognate with Scots efter (“after”), North Frisian efter (“after, behind”), West Frisian after, achter, efter (“behind; after”), Low German and Dutch achter (“behind”), German after- (“after-”), Danish and Swedish efter (“after”), Norwegian Bokmål and Norwegian Nynorsk etter (“after”), Faroese and Icelandic eftir (“after”).

senses.d: Behind; later in time; following.
ex: I left the room, and the dog bounded after.
They lived happily ever after.

senses.d: Subsequently to; following in time; later than.
ex: We had a few beers after the game.
The time is a quarter after eight.

senses.d: Subsequently to and as a result of.
ex: Sucess comes after hard work.

senses.d: Subsequently to and considering.
ex: I’m not putting you in charge again after the last disaster.

senses.d: Subsequently to and in spite of.
ex: After all that has happened, he is still my friend.
I can’t believe that, after all our advice against gambling, you walked into that casino!

senses.d: Subsequently to the actions of (someone), in order to remedy a situation.
ex: I'm tired of picking up after you. Why can't you clean your own messes?

senses.d: Repeatedly, seemingly in a sequence without end.
ex: day after day, time after time, mile after mile, beer after beer, smile after smile
Paper after paper spells out how vulnerable we are to internet-induced brain rot.

senses.d: Used to indicate recent completion of an activity.
ex: I was after finishing my dinner when there was a knock on the door. [= I had just finished my dinner when ...]

senses.d: Behind.
ex: He will leave a trail of destruction after him.
I told her to shut the door after her.

senses.d: In pursuit of, seeking; denoting the aim or object.
ex: run after him; he’s after a job; to thirst after righteousness

senses.d: Concerning; in relation to.
ex: to enquire after a friend; to ask after her health

senses.d: Signifies that the action of the clause it starts takes place before the action of the other clause.
ex: The show ends after the fat lady sings.
After we had decided to call it a day, I went home.

senses.d: Later; second (of two); next, following, subsequent
ex: The amends he had made in after life were lost sight of in the dramatic glare of the original act.

senses.d: At or towards the stern of a ship or the rear of an aircraft.
ex: The after gun is mounted aft.
The after gun is abaft the forward gun.

senses.d: Of before-and-after images: the one that shows the difference after a specified treatment.
ex: Did any of the before pictures remind you of yourself, and did any of the afters show what you hoped your results might be?

grp.label: subsequently; following in time; later than
in allusion to, in imitation of; following or referencing

ety.text: From Middle English afternone, after-non, equivalent to after- + noon.

senses.d: The part of the day from noon or lunchtime until sunset, evening, or suppertime or 6pm.
ex: Theſe men ſerue God in the forenoone, and the diuell in the after noone;
Here the stripped panelling was warmly gold and the pictures, mostly of the English school, were mellow and gentle in the afternoon light.

senses.d: The later part of anything, often with implications of decline.
A party or social event held in the afternoon.
In the afternoon.

senses.d: That which happens after, that which follows, usually of strongly negative connotation in most contexts, implying a preceding catastrophe.
ex: In contrast to most projections of the aftermath of nuclear war, in this there is no rioting or looting.

senses.d: A second mowing; the grass which grows after the first crop of hay in the same season.
ex: They were cutting aftermath on all sides, which gave the neighbourhood, this gusty autumn morning, an untimely smell of hay.
